[Elementary Statistics](../index.qmd) / Normal probability

## What does a probability tell us?

Suppose scores on a **hypothetical attention test** follow a normal distribution with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. What fraction of scores would you expect to be above 60? If we randomly generated many scores, would the observed fraction match that prediction?

This optional activity focuses on **normal probabilities and the connection between probability and repeated observations**, part of Week 5 in the proposed Elementary Statistics course. Conditional probability and independence will receive separate instruction.

::: {.normal-overview}

**Learning goals**

After this activity, you should be able to:

1. Interpret the shaded area under a normal curve as a probability.
2. Express a score as a z-score in standard deviation units.
3. Predict how changing a threshold changes a tail probability.
4. Explain why observed frequencies from repeated random draws are close to, but not always equal to, theoretical probabilities.

**Before starting:** Review the mean, standard deviation, and z-scores from Weeks 3 and 4.

:::

## Interpret what you find

1. Set the threshold to **60**, choose **above**, and draw 100 observations. Compare the observed percentage with the model's probability. Draw 1,000 more. Does it have to move closer every time?
2. Keep **above** selected, then change the threshold to **65** and **70**. What happens to the shaded probability?
3. Choose **below**, with the threshold at **50**. How does the normal curve's symmetry help you predict the probability?

## What is the normal model telling us?

For a normally distributed variable with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), a score \(x\) can be standardized as \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\). In this model, a score of 60 has \(z=(60-50)/10=1\), meaning it is one population standard deviation above the mean. The **area under the curve** to the right of 60 is approximately 15.9%, so \(P(X>60)\approx0.159\).

**Why this makes sense:** Scores near the middle are more common in this model than scores far into either tail. Moving a cutoff farther right leaves fewer scores above it. When we generate scores at random, the percentage above a cutoff may bounce around at first. With many independent draws, it tends to settle near the theoretical probability, although individual batches can still move it away.

The normal curve is a model, not a guarantee that real attention-test scores follow this shape. The simulation draws from the model deliberately so that the predicted and observed probabilities can be compared.
